newsitem.title: USA: Cleveland stadium important to city renewal-report.
newsitem.headline: Cleveland stadium important to city renewal-report.

text.p: Cleveland's $242.8 million football stadium project highlights economic development movement in the city from manufacturing to entertainment, tourism and services in recent years, A.G. Edwards & Sons Inc. said in its Bondline newsletter.

"While the stadium is a nonessential public project, we feel that it is an important piece in the puzzle of economic development in Cleveland," said A.G. Edwards, leader of a syndicate for the expected sale of $130 million of certificates of participation for the facility next week.
Officials held a ground-breaking ceremony for the new stadium earlier this week.

The facility, to be located on the site of the old Cleveland Municipal Stadium near Lake Erie, is expected to be completed on time for the city's new expansion Cleveland Browns football team to begin play in 1999.

The stadium project serves as an extension of economic development that has included the opening of a new baseball stadium, indoor arena, science museum and rock and roll hall of fame in the 1990s, A.G. Edwards said.

A major renovation of Cleveland Municipal Stadium had been planned even before the old Cleveland Browns left the city for Baltimore in 1995. On the eve of its departure, Cleveland residents authorized a series of taxes to pay for renovations.

The team's departure sparked litigation ultimately resolved with an agreement for the team nickname and colors to be held in trust for a new franchise that would play in a new stadium, paid for in part by the National Football League, which holds a lease to be assigned to the new team owner.

In addition to the COPs, the 72,000 seat stadium is to be financed with a $36 million contribution from Ohio, up to $48 million from the National Football League, a $10 million loan from the Cleveland Development Partnership and $20 million in non-tax revenu debt issued by the city of Cleveland, A.G. Edwards noted.
"As a result of the diverse commitments to this high-profile project, we feel that nonappropriation is not a likely option for the city should financial difficulties occur," A.G. Edwards said.
Moody's Investors Service has given the COPs an underlying Baa1 rating and Standard & Poor's Corp has assigned a BBB-plus.
